reviews.rationale: Upheld as a qualified whole-case conclusion on the supplied working texts. EO 7431 identifies George C. Havenner, liaison officer in the Government Printing Office, and is signed August 17, 1936 with closing number 7431. Its complete original contains one combined operative grant: exemption from section 204 and continuance in service until October 1, 1937. Both the recital and operative sentence give that date; the exact ending span 1276:1367 confirms it. The quoted statutory authority and September 1936 retirement-age recital add no independent command or concrete earlier-ending condition. October 1, 1937 is a direct temporal limit on this combined exemption/continuance, rather than merely a deadline requiring proof that service was performed. Earlier actual separation is unknown and not assumed to occur or not occur. EO 7704, signed September 10, 1937, expressly names the same person and prior order and separately grants further exemption/continuance until October 1, 1938. It contains no express revocation, substituted date or direction amending EO 7431; the later signing date and later cap therefore do not replace the original grant's own limit or prove uninterrupted employment. No independent surviving command or savings clause appears. Possible accrued employment effects do not preserve the original operative authority. The claimed first_end and whole_order_end calendar date 1937-10-01 and terminated/no-current-operative-force conclusion at October 14, 2026 are supported within the stated bounded source coverage. No formal revocation or universal lifecycle search completeness is certified.

reviews.rationale: Rejected as an exact whole-case claim because the asserted ending contradicts its own byte-verified source. EO 7420 identifies William T. Marshall, office-man in the Federal Emergency Administration of Public Works, with closing number 7420 and signing line July 20, 1936. That is its signing date, not its operative ending. The complete original repeats until August 1, 1937 in the retirement recital and in the operative exemption/continuance sentence; the cited exact span 1325:1386 reads thereof and continue him in the service until August 1, 1937. Nevertheless first_end.date and whole_order_end.date are 1936-07-20, and the judgment, source-note description and research rationale repeatedly misstate that signing date as the operative limit. An internally mixed member check also mentions August 1, which does not cure those exact false conclusions. No evidence establishes service cessation or an earlier legal ending on July 20, 1936. EO 7629, signed June 8, 1937, expressly recites EO 7420 and the same employee/position, and makes a separate further exemption/continuance until August 1, 1938. Neither its signing date nor its new cap changes the original text into a July 20, 1936 sunset; it also does not prove uninterrupted actual service. The original has one combined temporary grant, no concrete separate earlier-ending condition, no independent surviving command and no savings clause preserving operative force. The reported no-current-operative-force conclusion is compatible with a long-expired calendar grant, but it cannot uphold this exact lifecycle record with its materially wrong first and whole-order ending dates. The claim is not repaired by this review.
